To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
family-based psychosocial interventions are beneficial for the patient and the family member, but the effects are small and the evidence base is weak.
family-based interventions are more effective than usual medical care in reducing depression among patients with chronic illness.

interventions targeting the patient's spouse have positive effects on patient outcomes, interventions targeting the patient have positive effects on family member outcomes, and interventions targeting both the patient and family member have positive effects on both patient and family outcomes.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new generation of interventions that can improve the quality of life of people with chronic illnesses and their family members.
the role of family relationships in the course of chronic illness and with the effects of family-focused interventions.
the development and evaluation of interventions to improve the quality of family life for people with dementia and their carers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of family interventions are small and not very consistent.
the evidence base for family interventions in chronic illness is weak.
the evidence is not strong enough to recommend family interventions in the absence of a clear need.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the involvement of family members in interventions is beneficial to the patients, but not to the family members themselves.
it is beneficial to involve a patient's family member in the treatment process, particularly if the family member is the spouse.
family members are an important part of the treatment team and can have a positive effect on the patient.
The main takeaway from our work is that

interventions that involve family members may be more effective than those that do not, and that the most effective interventions are those that target the family member alone and that address relationship issues.
it's not a one size fits all approach.
it is important to consider the family member when developing psychosocial interventions.
